```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
ch_rainfall <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1wYLHVVsemxQVjsdsmSzV9m0G6eLR_YK4", show_col_types = FALSE)
pm_nc <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=19Axv5_bv7p4LbDWNDs4TmdFi3gfYeNXc", show_col_types = FALSE)
rdu_jan <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ABpiu5ABzAo-WXbYBp9LWgN8-lHuFQR9", show_col_types = FALSE)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
n_rain_rows <- nrow(ch_rainfall)
n_rain_dates <- n_distinct(ch_rainfall$date)
rain_years <- range(lubridate::year(ch_rainfall$date))
jan_years <- range(lubridate::year(rdu_jan$date))
```

## Part 1 · Run-through {#run-through}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1 · Load the data

::: {.why}
Three datasets: daily rainfall in Chapel Hill (`r rain_years[1]` to `r rain_years[2]`, from the [NC State Climate Office](https://products.climate.ncsu.edu/data/)), daily PM2.5 across North Carolina (2016 to 2020, from the [CDC Environmental Public Health Tracking Network](https://ephtracking.cdc.gov/)), and daily January highs at RDU airport (`r jan_years[1]` to `r jan_years[2]`, from the [Iowa Environmental Mesonet](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/request/download.phtml)).
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#daily rainfall in Chapel Hill
ch_rainfall <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1wYLHVVsemxQVjsdsmSzV9m0G6eLR_YK4")

#daily PM2.5 across North Carolina, 2016-2020
pm_nc <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=19Axv5_bv7p4LbDWNDs4TmdFi3gfYeNXc")

#daily January high temperatures at RDU
rdu_jan <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ABpiu5ABzAo-WXbYBp9LWgN8-lHuFQR9")
```

### Step 2 · Make one row per day

::: {.why}
Probability counts days, so each row must be one day. The rainfall file has `r format(n_rain_rows, big.mark = ",")` rows but only `r format(n_rain_dates, big.mark = ",")` distinct dates: some dates were recorded twice. We keep one row per date, and count the day as rainy if either record shows rain.
:::

```{r}
#one row per date, keeping the larger rainfall value
ch_daily <- ch_rainfall |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(prec_in = max(prec_in))

#flag rainy days (1 = any rain, 0 = none)
ch_daily <- ch_daily |> mutate(rain = ifelse(prec_in > 0, 1, 0))
```

::: {.reading}
**Why it matters.** Always ask what one row represents before you count anything. Duplicate rows would count some days twice.
:::

### Step 3 · Empirical probability

::: {.why}
Empirical probability is the share of observed days on which the event happened: **P(E) = f / n**, where f is the number of days the event happened and n is the number of days observed.
:::

```{r}
#share of days with any rain
p_rain <- sum(ch_daily$rain) / nrow(ch_daily)
p_rain
```

::: {.reading}
**What it tells us.** About `r round(100 * p_rain)`% of days in the record had some rain, roughly one day in three.
:::

### Step 4 · Empirical probability at many places

::: {.why}
The same formula works for every location at once if we group first. Here each row of `pm_nc` is one day in one census tract (a modelled estimate at the tract centre), so we flag days with moderate or worse air quality (a daily PM2.5 above 9.0 µg/m³, the EPA "moderate" line since 2024), then count f and n for each location.
:::

```{r, message = FALSE}
#flag moderate or worse days (1 = PM2.5 above 9.0, 0 = not)
flagged_pm <- pm_nc |> mutate(aq_flag = ifelse(pm_val > 9, 1, 0))

#f and n for each location, then P(E) = f / n
pm_prob <- flagged_pm |>
  group_by(lat, lon) |>
  summarise(tot_flag = sum(aq_flag), tot_ob = n()) |>
  mutate(p_bad_air = tot_flag / tot_ob)

#turn it into a spatial object: longitude (x) goes first, then latitude (y)
pm_prob_sf <- pm_prob |> st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

#map the probability at each location
tm_shape(pm_prob_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "p_bad_air", size = 0.3,
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "P(moderate or worse)"))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
pm_range <- range(pm_prob$p_bad_air)
```

::: {.reading}
**What it tells us.** Across `r format(nrow(pm_prob), big.mark = ",")` tracts, the chance of a moderate or worse air day ranges from `r fmt(pm_range[1])` to `r fmt(pm_range[2])`. If the points don't fall in North Carolina, check the order inside `coords =`: longitude comes first.
:::

### Step 5 · Binomial distribution

::: {.why}
The binomial distribution counts "successes" across a fixed number of trials, where each trial has two outcomes (rain or no rain) and the same probability. Rain isn't really independent from day to day, and it varies by season, so treat this as a simplifying model.
:::

```{r}
#probability of 0 through 10 rainy days in 10 days
probability_days <- tibble(
  num_days = 0:10,
  probability = dbinom(x = 0:10, size = 10, prob = p_rain)
)

#plot the distribution
ggplot(probability_days, aes(x = num_days, y = probability)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
most_likely <- probability_days |> slice_max(probability)
p_zero <- dbinom(0, 10, p_rain)
```

::: {.reading}
**What it tells us.** The most likely outcome is `r most_likely$num_days` rainy days (`r fmt(most_likely$probability)`). A dry stretch of 10 days is rare: `dbinom(0, 10, p_rain)` is `r fmt(p_zero)`, about 1 in `r round(1 / p_zero)`.
:::

### Step 6 · Cumulative probability

::: {.why}
`pbinom(q, size, p)` gives the probability of **q or fewer**. Questions are often worded the other way, so translate the words first.
:::

| Question says | Which outcomes | Code | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 days or fewer | 0 to 3 | `pbinom(3, 10, p_rain)` | `r fmt(pbinom(3, 10, p_rain))` |
| more than 3 days | 4 to 10 | `1 - pbinom(3, 10, p_rain)` | `r fmt(1 - pbinom(3, 10, p_rain))` |
| at least 3 days | 3 to 10 | `1 - pbinom(2, 10, p_rain)` | `r fmt(1 - pbinom(2, 10, p_rain))` |

::: {.reading}
**What it tells us.** "More than 3" and "at least 3" differ by a whole bar of the chart, here `r fmt(dbinom(3, 10, p_rain))`. Part 2 uses "more than 3".
:::

### Step 7 · Normal distribution

::: {.why}
A continuous variable like temperature can be modelled with a normal curve built from its mean and standard deviation.
:::

```{r}
#mean and standard deviation of January highs
jan_mean <- mean(rdu_jan$max_temp)
jan_sd <- sd(rdu_jan$max_temp)

#normal model: probability of a high of 60 or above
1 - pnorm(60, mean = jan_mean, sd = jan_sd)

#empirical check: share of observed days at 60 or above
mean(rdu_jan$max_temp >= 60)

#histogram of the data with the normal curve on top
ggplot(rdu_jan, aes(x = max_temp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 4, boundary = 0) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = jan_mean, sd = jan_sd)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, linetype = "dashed")
```

::: {.reading}
**What it tells us.** The normal model says `r round(100 * (1 - pnorm(60, jan_mean, jan_sd)))`% of January days reach 60°F; the record says `r round(100 * mean(rdu_jan$max_temp >= 60))`%. The curve fits the middle well but misses in the tails, so be careful using it for rare events. `pnorm()` gives the share *below* a value, which is why we subtract from 1 for "above".
:::

### Check yourselves before splitting up

1. What does one row of `ch_daily` represent, and why did we have to make that true?
2. Your partner says "at least 2 rainy days" and writes `1 - pbinom(2, 10, p_rain)`. What should they write instead?

### Partner A · Flood-risk days at Bolin Creek

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#USGS gauge readings, 2015-2025
bolin_creek_data <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1eEzriJ5XzR-aS74nJmyiQFVrmV4T3cel")
```

1. Make one row per day by keeping each day's highest water reading. *(Step 2)*
2. A flood-risk day is one where the water is more than 1 ft above the median daily height. Flag those days and find the empirical probability. *(Steps 2 and 3)*
3. Find the most likely number of flood-risk days in a 25-day period. *(Step 5)*
4. Find the probability of **more than 3** flood-risk days in 25 days. *(Step 6)*

**Bring to Part 3:** your daily probability and your answer to item 4.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B · Cold January days across NC

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#January highs at 42 ASOS stations, 2000-2019
asos_jan_data <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1_zE1kcC7YY083R6rv20sqeN1l2dCdmhi")
```

1. Group by station and find each station's mean and standard deviation of January highs. *(Steps 4 and 7)*
2. Use the normal model to find each station's probability of a high **below 40°F**. *(Step 7)*
3. Map the probabilities. *(Step 4: longitude goes first)*
4. Pick the station with the highest probability east of the mountains (longitude east of -80).

**Bring to Part 3:** that station's name and its daily probability.
:::
::::

2. Partner B explains to Partner A why the normal model might over- or underestimate cold days at that station (look back at Step 7).
3. Decide together which hazard deserves planning first, and what your numbers can't tell you (for example, how bad each event is).

## Answer key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
#Partner A
bolin_creek_data <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1eEzriJ5XzR-aS74nJmyiQFVrmV4T3cel", show_col_types = FALSE)
bolin_daily <- bolin_creek_data |> group_by(time) |> summarise(max_water = max(value))
median_height <- median(bolin_daily$max_water)
p_flood <- mean(bolin_daily$max_water > median_height + 1)
flood_mode <- which.max(dbinom(0:25, 25, p_flood)) - 1
flood_more3 <- 1 - pbinom(3, 25, p_flood)

#Partner B
asos_jan_data <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1_zE1kcC7YY083R6rv20sqeN1l2dCdmhi", show_col_types = FALSE)
station_cold <- asos_jan_data |>
  group_by(station) |>
  summarise(n_days = n(),
            p_cold = pnorm(40, mean(max_temp), sd(max_temp)),
            emp_cold = mean(max_temp < 40),
            lon = first(lon)) |>
  arrange(desc(p_cold))
top_east <- station_cold |> filter(lon > -80) |> slice_max(p_cold)
top_all <- station_cold |> slice_max(p_cold)
short_stations <- station_cold |> filter(n_days < 100)
cold_more3 <- 1 - pbinom(3, 25, top_east$p_cold)
n_under <- sum(station_cold$p_cold < station_cold$emp_cold)
```

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Bolin Creek median daily max | `r median_height` ft |
| A: flood-risk probability per day | `r fmt(p_flood)` |
| A: most likely count in 25 days | `r flood_mode` (probability `r fmt(dbinom(flood_mode, 25, p_flood))`) |
| A: P(more than 3 in 25) | `r fmt(flood_more3)` |
| B: highest station east of -80 | `r top_east$station`, `r fmt(top_east$p_cold)` |
| B: highest overall (mountains) | `r top_all$station`, `r fmt(top_all$p_cold)` |
| Joint: P(more than 3 cold days in 25) at `r top_east$station` | `r fmt(cold_more3)` |

**What a good card says.** Cold days are the more likely problem (`r fmt(cold_more3)` vs `r fmt(flood_more3)` for more than 3 days in 25), but the numbers say nothing about how damaging each event is. The normal model gives a lower chance of a high below 40°F than the record does at `r n_under` of `r nrow(station_cold)` stations, so it tends to understate cold days.

`r if (nrow(short_stations) > 0) paste0("Most stations have about 600 January days in the file, but some have far fewer: ", paste0(short_stations$station, " (", short_stations$n_days, ")", collapse = ", "), ". If a pair picks one of these, ask whether they trust that estimate.")`

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#### Partner A: flood-risk days at Bolin Creek ####
bolin_creek_data <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1eEzriJ5XzR-aS74nJmyiQFVrmV4T3cel")

#A1: one row per day, keeping each day's highest reading (Step 2)
bolin_daily <- bolin_creek_data |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(max_water = max(value))

#A2: flood-risk day = more than 1 ft above the median daily height (Steps 2-3)
median_height <- median(bolin_daily$max_water)
bolin_daily <- bolin_daily |>
  mutate(flood_risk = ifelse(max_water > median_height + 1, 1, 0))
p_flood <- sum(bolin_daily$flood_risk) / nrow(bolin_daily)
p_flood

#A3: most likely number of flood-risk days in 25 days (Step 5)
flood_dist <- tibble(num_days = 0:25,
                     probability = dbinom(0:25, size = 25, prob = p_flood))
flood_dist |> slice_max(probability)

#A4: probability of MORE THAN 3 flood-risk days in 25 (Step 6)
1 - pbinom(3, size = 25, prob = p_flood)

#### Partner B: cold January days across NC ####
asos_jan_data <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1_zE1kcC7YY083R6rv20sqeN1l2dCdmhi")

#B1-B2: per-station mean and sd, then normal-model P(high below 40F) (Step 7)
station_cold <- asos_jan_data |>
  group_by(station) |>
  summarise(n_days = n(),
            jan_mean = mean(max_temp),
            jan_sd = sd(max_temp),
            p_cold = pnorm(40, mean = jan_mean, sd = jan_sd),
            lat = first(lat),
            lon = first(lon)) |>
  arrange(desc(p_cold))
station_cold

#B3: map it (longitude goes first, Step 4)
station_sf <- st_as_sf(station_cold, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
tm_shape(station_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "p_cold", size = 0.8,
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "P(high < 40°F)"))

#B4: highest probability east of the mountains (longitude east of -80)
station_cold |>
  filter(lon > -80) |>
  slice_max(p_cold)

#### Part 3: together ####
p_cold_station <- station_cold |>
  filter(lon > -80) |>
  slice_max(p_cold) |>
  pull(p_cold)

#P(more than 3 cold days in a 25-day stretch)
1 - pbinom(3, size = 25, prob = p_cold_station)
```
